evidence.claim: Mountain gaps and waterfalls frame a loop through the Chattahoochee headwaters.
evidence.quote: the Russell-Brasstown Scenic Byway encircles the headwaters of the Chattahoochee River

evidence.claim: Mountain gaps and waterfalls frame a loop through the Chattahoochee headwaters.
evidence.quote: the byway winds through the valleys and mountain gaps of the southern Appalachians. From the vistas atop Brasstown Bald to the cooling mists of waterfalls

evidence.claim: The Russell–Brasstown byway winds through southern Appalachian valleys and mountain gaps within the Chattahoochee National Forest.
evidence.quote: Surrounded by the beauty of the Chattahoochee National Forest, the byway winds through the valleys and mountain gaps of the southern Appalachians.

evidence.claim: Its loop encircles the Chattahoochee River headwaters; the Forest Service gives the drive as 40 miles and recommends at least three hours.
evidence.quote: The 40-mile loop follows State Highways 348, 180, and 17/75. Allow at least three hours driving time.

evidence.claim: A National Scenic Byway since June 15, 2000, it includes Georgia’s highest mountain, Brasstown Bald.
evidence.quote: The Russell-Brasstown route was awarded National Scenic Byway Designation on June 15, 2000. This route includes Brasstown Bald, Georgia's highest mountain.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service highlights wildflowers, fall color and views into wilderness valleys.
evidence.quote: The drive is ideal for viewing colorful wildflowers or dazzling fall color. Secluded valley views of Wilderness Areas abound along the way.

evidence.claim: The loop came together through improvements to several numbered roads.
evidence.quote: the Russell–Brasstown Scenic Byway is composed of parts or entire lengths of numbered routes.

evidence.claim: Its SR 75 section was established in 1932 and paved by the end of 1946.
evidence.quote: The portion of SR 75 included in the byway was established between May and August 1932 along the same alignment as it travels today.

evidence.claim: Its SR 75 section was established in 1932 and paved by the end of 1946.
evidence.quote: By the end of 1946, the above-mentioned segment of SR 75 was paved.

evidence.claim: In 1966, two parts of SR 348 were joined, completing a paved circuit.
evidence.quote: Later that year, both parts of SR 348 were connected, and the entire byway was paved.

evidence.claim: In 1966, two parts of SR 348 were joined, completing a paved circuit.
evidence.quote: By 1966, the byway's entire segment of SR 180 was paved. Also, SR 348 was established in two parts.

evidence.claim: National Forest Scenic Byway designation followed in 1989.
evidence.quote: The Russell–Brasstown Scenic Byway was designated as a National Forest Scenic Byway on June 5, 1989.

evidence.claim: Before that final connection, the SR 75 section had progressed from graded earth to a semi-hard surface by July 1939. Paving and the joining of SR 348 preceded the later scenic designations: the touring route inherited roads built in stages.
evidence.quote: By July 1939, this section of SR 75 was converted from "completed grading, not surfaced" to "completed semi-hard surface".

evidence.claim: For a circuit beginning at Brasstown Bald, descend the spur to SR 180 and take the eastern side toward SR 17/75.
evidence.quote: On SR-180 SPUR, from the Brasstown Bald Visitor Center, to SR-180;

evidence.claim: For a circuit beginning at Brasstown Bald, descend the spur to SR 180 and take the eastern side toward SR 17/75.
evidence.quote: From there, it follows SR 17/SR 75 north to a junction with SR 180 in the Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest. The byway turns west on SR 180 with an optional detour to the Brasstown Bald Visitor Center on SR 180 Spur.

evidence.claim: Head south toward Helen, then use SR 75 Alternate to reach SR 348.
evidence.quote: The byway forms a loop starting northwest of Helen, at the junction of SR 17/SR 75 and SR 75 Alternate.

evidence.claim: Head south toward Helen, then use SR 75 Alternate to reach SR 348.
evidence.quote: then southeast back to SR 75 Alternate before turning northeast, back to SR 17/SR 75.

evidence.claim: Follow SR 348 northwest to Choestoe and SR 180 back toward the summit spur.
evidence.quote: It follows SR 180 westward and southwestward to SR 348 (Richard B. Russell Scenic Highway) in Choestoe and then southeast back to SR 75 Alternate before turning northeast, back to SR 17/SR 75.

evidence.claim: Brasstown Bald is Georgia’s highest point, known to the Cherokee people as Enotah.
evidence.quote: Brasstown Bald or Enotah is the highest point in the U.S. state of Georgia.

evidence.claim: Brasstown Bald is Georgia’s highest point, known to the Cherokee people as Enotah.
evidence.quote: The mountain is known to the native Cherokee people as Enotah.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service describes a summit view spanning 360 degrees of rolling highlands.
evidence.quote: Linger atop Brasstown Bald, Georgia's tallest mountain, to absorb all 360-degrees of rolling highlands

evidence.claim: The mountain also carries a monument to someone who worked to bring visitors here: former Georgia Supreme Court Judge Thomas S. Candler.
evidence.quote: Former Georgia Supreme Court Judge Thomas S. Candler is memorialized with a stone monument at Brasstown Bald.

evidence.claim: Erected in 1971, three months before his death, the stone recognizes his support for attracting visitors and establishing a visitor center.
evidence.quote: It was erected in 1971 three months before he died in recognition of his efforts to support getting more visitors to the mountain and establishing a visitor center there for them.

evidence.claim: On a clear day, the tallest buildings in Atlanta can be seen from the summit, some 85 miles away.
evidence.quote: On a clear day it is possible to see the tallest buildings of Atlanta, some 85 miles away from the summit.

evidence.claim: Dukes Creek Falls carries one creek’s name but drops on another: Davis Creek, at its meeting with Dukes Creek.
evidence.quote: The 150 foot Dukes Creek Falls, which are actually located on Davis Creek at its confluence with Dukes Creek

evidence.claim: An observation platform faces the falls.
evidence.quote: There is an observation platform at the falls.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service describes a 2.2-mile round-trip path to the pool below the cascade.
evidence.quote: a 2.2 mile-long round trip hiking path delivers you to a misty poolside below a cascading waterfall.

evidence.claim: Dukes Creek also belongs to the story of Georgia’s gold rush. Gold was found in the creek in 1828; discoveries in White County and neighboring Lumpkin County led to the rush.
evidence.quote: Dukes Creek is the creek in White County, Georgia, on which gold was found in 1828. The discovery of gold in White County and neighboring Lumpkin County led to the Georgia Gold Rush.

evidence.claim: Beyond the falls, Dukes Creek flows into the Chattahoochee southeast of Helen, joining the river whose headwaters the byway encircles.
evidence.quote: flows into the Chattahoochee River just east of the intersection between State Route 17 and State Route 75 southeast of Helen.

evidence.claim: The falls drop on Davis Creek where it meets Dukes Creek.
evidence.quote: The 150 foot Dukes Creek Falls, which are actually located on Davis Creek at its confluence with Dukes Creek

evidence.claim: At Hogpen Gap, the byway crosses the Appalachian Trail, a meeting of the driving route and the footpath identified by the Forest Service.
evidence.quote: Cross the famed Appalachian Trail at Hogpen Gap.
